title: Aamir Khan Personally Knocked on a Door to Steal a Title. That Film Is Now Bollywood's Biggest Independence Day Bet.
excerpt: Batwara — formerly Lahore 1947 — stars Sunny Deol and his son Karan in their first-ever scene together. The teaser drops June 15. A Father's Day promo follows six days later. Here's everything we know.
body:
There is a moment in the making of every big Bollywood film where the project stops being a movie and starts becoming an event. For **Batwara**, that moment might have been the afternoon **Aamir Khan** showed up at the home of a late producer's family, sat with the man's widow and son, and asked to buy the rights to a title.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=XWFUvTdz7Zg</youtube>

The title was *Batwara*. The original 1989 film by **J.P. Dutta** starred Dharmendra and Vinod Khanna. The family that owned the rights — the family of the late producer **Salim Akhtar** — hadn't been expecting India's most meticulous superstar at their door.

> Aamir told the family about his wonderful experience of working with Salim Akhtar in *Baazi* (1995). He also informed them about his film and how the title *Batwara* is apt for the subject. — Bollywood Hungama

Veteran filmmaker **Karim Morani** arranged the meeting. Aamir met Akhtar's son **Samad** and his mother **Shama**. The deal was done the way Aamir does everything: personally, respectfully, with homework done.

## From Lahore 1947 to Batwara

The film was announced as **Lahore 1947**, a name that made geographic sense for a Partition drama set in the city. But the team — led by director **Rajkumar Santoshi**, reuniting with Sunny Deol for the first time in nearly three decades — felt the title was too literal, too narrow for the emotional territory the film covers.

They tried *Batwara 1947*. Then simply *Batwara* — a word that means division, splitting, partition in the most visceral, human sense. Not a city name. Not a year. A wound.

The film is based on **Asghar Wajahat's** iconic 1980 play *Jis Lahore Nai Dekhya* (*He Who Hasn't Seen Lahore*). The story follows a Muslim family migrating from Lucknow to Lahore during Partition, only to find an elderly Hindu matriarch refusing to leave her ancestral haveli. It's a story about what happens when history draws a line through someone's living room.

## Sunny and Karan: The Real Father-Son Act

Here's the detail that makes this film irresistible: **Sunny Deol** and his son **Karan Deol** will share the screen for the very first time. Sunny directed Karan's debut *Pal Pal Dil Ke Paas* in 2019, but they never acted together — until now.

The makers know what they have. A **special Father's Day promo** is being designed specifically around the Sunny-Karan dynamic and is planned for release on **June 21**. Before that, the film's official **teaser drops on June 15**.

According to Bollywood Hungama, the father and son share "an interesting dynamic" in the film — which, given that the story deals with generational trauma, displacement, and the things families carry across borders, should hit in exactly the right places.

## A Cast That Demands Attention

The lineup reads like a Bollywood reunion summit:

- **Sunny Deol** — the man whose career was built on Partition dramas (*Gadar*, *Border*)
- **Preity Zinta** — returning to the big screen in a role that reportedly gives her serious dramatic range
- **Shabana Azmi** — the matriarch of Indian cinema playing, quite possibly, a literal matriarch
- **Ali Fazal** — fresh off a stacked 2026 lineup
- **Karan Deol** — his third film, his first alongside his father
- **Aamir Khan** — in a supporting role, producing and acting, because that's how Aamir does things

Behind the camera: **A.R. Rahman** on music. **Javed Akhtar** on lyrics. **Santosh Sivan** behind the camera. **Resul Pookutty** on sound. This isn't a film. It's a summit meeting of Indian cinema's finest craftspeople.

## Why the Diaspora Should Circle August 13

**Batwara** releases on **August 13, 2026** — right in the Independence Day window, which has traditionally been the launchpad for Bollywood's most patriotic, emotionally charged blockbusters.

For NRIs whose grandparents lived through Partition, whose families still argue about what was left behind — a house, a neighbourhood, a life — this film is positioned to be more than entertainment. It's a mirror held up to history that many diaspora families still carry in silence.

Two promos in June. A release in August. Aamir Khan's fingerprints on every detail. Keep your eyes on this one.
